title: LIMS vs ELN vs ERP: Key Differences and Which Systems Your Lab Needs
summary: LIMS vs ELN vs ERP explained: what each system owns, where they overlap, when your lab needs all three, and how to connect them without duplicating lab data.
body_markdown:
## **TL;DR**


- ‍ **LIMS** manages samples, tests, results, and repeatable laboratory workflows.
- ‍ **ELN** documents experiments, protocols, observations, and scientific reasoning. **‍**
- **ERP** manages broader business operations, including procurement, finance, suppliers, and resource planning.
- Most growing labs need all three, so the real decision is which system owns each record and how data moves between them.


LIMS, ELN, and ERP get compared as if a lab must pick one. In practice, they answer different questions. A LIMS tells you where a sample is and what was tested. An ELN tells you why an experiment was run and what the scientist concluded. An ERP tells you what it cost, who supplied it, and when to reorder.


This guide compares the three side by side, covers the two most common head-to-head questions (LIMS vs ELN and LIMS vs ERP), and gives a practical way to decide what your lab needs and how the systems should connect.

## What Is the Difference Between LIMS, ELN, and ERP?


A LIMS (laboratory information management system) manages structured, repeatable lab work around samples and tests. An ELN (electronic lab notebook) documents experiments and scientific reasoning. An ERP (enterprise resource planning) system manages company-wide business processes such as finance, procurement, and inventory. They overlap at the edges, but each has a different center of gravity.


**Comparison** **LIMS** **ELN** **ERP**


Primary purpose Manage laboratory samples and workflows Document experiments and scientific context Manage enterprise resources and business processes


Core record Sample, test, result Experiment, protocol, observation Purchase order, supplier, financial or inventory record


Typical users Lab operations, analysts, QC teams Scientists, researchers, R&D teams Finance, procurement, operations, leadership


Common workflows Sample intake, testing, result review, reporting Experiment planning, documentation, analysis Purchasing, budgeting, invoicing, resource planning


Key integration Instruments, ELN, reporting systems LIMS, instruments, scientific data tools Finance, procurement, inventory, manufacturing systems


Best fit Structured, repeatable lab processes Exploratory and documented scientific work Organization-wide operational planning


### What a LIMS does


A[LIMS](https://www.scispot.com/lims) registers samples, assigns tests, tracks status and location, captures instrument results, and produces reports with an audit trail. It suits work where many samples follow defined methods, such as QC, contract testing, diagnostics, and biobanking. For a deeper primer, see[what a laboratory information management system is](https://www.scispot.com/blog/laboratory-information-management-system) .


### What an ELN does


An[electronic lab notebook](https://www.scispot.com/elns) replaces the paper notebook. Scientists record plans, procedures, observations, files, and conclusions, then share and search that history. It suits R&D, where protocols change and the narrative matters as much as the number.


### What an ERP does


An ERP connects finance, purchasing, suppliers, manufacturing, and enterprise inventory across the company. It knows what a reagent cost and which vendor shipped it. It does not natively understand aliquots, plate layouts, method versions, or a failed QC run. For life sciences options, see our guide to[ERP software for life sciences](https://www.scispot.com/blog/best-erp-software-for-life-sciences) .


## LIMS vs ELN: Where Research Records End and Lab Operations Begin


The LIMS vs ELN question is the one most labs hit first. The simplest test: if the unit of work is a sample moving through a defined process, it belongs in a LIMS. If the unit of work is an experiment whose design may change, it belongs in an ELN.


### When an ELN is the better fit


Choose an ELN first when work is exploratory, protocols evolve weekly, and you need a searchable record of decisions for collaboration, reproducibility, and IP. Early discovery and assay development teams usually start here.


### When a LIMS is the better fit


Choose a LIMS first when sample volume is high, methods are standardized, and you need chain of custody, test assignment, instrument data capture, and consistent reporting. Regulated testing and service labs usually start here.


### Why many R&D labs run both


Once discovery work produces samples that move into scale-up, QC, or external testing, the two records need to meet. The ELN holds the experiment; the LIMS holds the samples and results it produced. Linking them avoids re-typing IDs and keeps results tied to the protocol version that generated them. If you are moving data between them, plan the[ELN to LIMS data mapping](https://www.scispot.com/blog/eln-to-lims-migration-data-mapping-version-history-and-standard-operating-procedures) early.


## LIMS vs ERP: Can an ERP Replace a LIMS?


No. A LIMS is not an ERP system. Some ERPs include quality or batch modules that cover simple testing in a manufacturing context, but they are built around orders, items, and ledgers rather than samples, methods, and instrument files.


### Where ERP falls short in the lab


Common gaps include sample-level chain of custody, instrument data capture, method and specification versioning, result review workflows, and lab-specific audit trails. Teams that force these into an ERP often end up with spreadsheets alongside it.


### When to integrate LIMS and ERP


Integrate when the systems share materials, orders, costs, or status. Typical flows are purchase orders and receipts from ERP into the lab, and consumption, completed tests, or billable work from the lab back to ERP. Our guide to[LIMS integration with ERP and other systems](https://www.scispot.com/blog/lims-integration-benefits-types-and-steps) covers the steps.


## How to Choose the Right Mix of LIMS, ELN, and ERP


Start from your records and workflows, not product categories. Vendor feature lists overlap heavily; ownership of data does not.


### Choose LIMS when sample tracking is the main challenge


Consider a LIMS if your team struggles to track sample locations, assign tests, standardize procedures, connect instrument results, or maintain a reliable record of sample status.


For example, a quality control laboratory may need every incoming sample linked to a defined test, acceptance criteria, analyst activity, review status, and final report.


### Choose ELN when experiment documentation is the priority


An ELN may be the better starting point when scientists conduct exploratory research, frequently adjust experimental methods, or need to capture detailed observations and reasoning.


For example, a biotech R&D team comparing experimental conditions needs to document what changed between runs, which materials were used, what was observed, and how the team interpreted the findings.


### Choose ERP when business coordination is the main gap


ERP is important when the problem extends beyond scientific work—for example, connecting purchasing, supplier management, budgets, inventory valuation, or manufacturing plans across departments.


A growing organization may need to connect planned material purchases and actual consumption with laboratory activity, while keeping finance and procurement records in the ERP.

## How LIMS, ELN, and ERP Work Together


### Follow a real laboratory workflow


Consider a biotech company running experiments that consume reagents and generate results.


1. **ERP:** A purchase order is created for reagents, with supplier and financial details maintained in the business system.
2. **LIMS:** Materials or samples are registered, identified, and tracked through defined laboratory workflows.
3. **ELN:** Scientists document the experimental protocol, conditions, observations, and interpretation, linking records to relevant samples.
4. **LIMS and ELN:** Relevant sample identifiers, results, and experiment references are linked so teams can trace the work across systems.
5. **ERP:** Where supported and needed, approved consumption, purchasing requirements, or operational data can feed business planning and inventory processes.


The exact sequence depends on the organization. Not every lab needs every handoff, and not every field should be synchronized between every application.


### Define which system owns each record


Integration works best when teams decide where each record is created, maintained, reviewed, and corrected.


For example:


- The ERP may own supplier and purchase-order records.
- The LIMS may own sample identifiers, test assignments, and laboratory result status.
- The ELN may own experiment narratives, protocols, and scientific observations.


These are common patterns, not universal rules. Your configuration should reflect your quality processes, data governance, and existing architecture.


### Reduce manual handoffs between systems


Disconnected tools can leave employees copying sample IDs, re-entering results, reconciling material usage, or transferring files manually. These handoffs create opportunities for inconsistencies and make it harder to understand where information originated.

## Connect Your Lab Systems Without Adding More Silos


LIMS, ELN, and ERP are not interchangeable, and a laboratory does not always need to choose only one. Each has a different role: managing structured laboratory operations, preserving scientific context, or coordinating business resources.


The goal is to build a system landscape that fits your workflows and keeps information connected without duplicating effort.
